video_title: WARNING: Bitcoin & Stocks Are Going MUCH Higher
gist: 42 Macro's Darius Dale tells Anthony Pompliano that a geopolitically driven supply-demand imbalance in Treasuries (the Treasury now needs ~40% of global savings vs ~20% pre-COVID) forces ever more policy intervention, which combined with the AI capex boom keeps US stocks at or near all-time highs for the next 12-18 months. Dale expects 'paradigm C' (grow out of the debt) to last to at least 2028 before sliding into money printing, and warns of rising political realignment risk; despite the title, Bitcoin gets only passing mention.

insights.claim: Darius Dale calls the fact that Treasury bonds are no longer considered a safe-haven asset the 'PC1' (primary driver) of all global finance, driven by a geopolitically induced supply-demand imbalance in the Treasury market.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Implies structurally higher term premia and continued search for alternative stores of value (gold, Bitcoin) over long-duration Treasuries.
insights.quote: the PC1 of all of global finance is the fact that treasury bonds are no longer considered to be a safe haven asset.

insights.claim: According to Darius Dale, the US Treasury needs over $12 trillion over the next year (roughly $10-12T refinancing, ~$2T new deficit, ~$125B refinancing into higher rates), up from under $5T pre-COVID, equal to about 40% of global savings flows versus ~20% on average before COVID.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Crowding-out of private credit supports wider mortgage and credit spreads and persistent inflation pressure.
insights.quote: that's 40% of global savings, the flow of global savings over the next year. That used to be on average 20% of the flow of global savings prior to CO.

insights.claim: Dale notes foreigners own ~30% of the Treasury market and the price-sensitive private non-bank sector now owns ~60%, up from 36% at end-2021, so each incremental unit of supply demands higher ex-ante yields; the US also runs a 3-4% of GDP current account deficit it must fund annually.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Shift toward price-sensitive holders makes long yields more sensitive to issuance, raising odds of intervention (buybacks, YCC).

insights.claim: Dale says the spread between the marginal mortgage rate and the effective rate on existing mortgages is about 250 basis points, roughly an all-time wide, driving housing lock-in, which he links to the Treasury absorbing the ~20% of global savings that used to fund mortgages and small-business lending.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Housing turnover and home-price weakness should persist while Treasury funding needs stay elevated.

insights.claim: Anthony Pompliano describes a 'full-on panic' among US home sellers as mortgage rates tick up and prices get slashed, arguing boomer-owned 20-30-year-old suburban homes are a product younger buyers neither want nor can afford.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Downside risk to older suburban home prices; homeowner resistance makes housing-affordability policy politically hard.
insights.quote: there is a full-on panic in this country of anyone trying to sell their home

insights.claim: Darius Dale says we are in a fiscal dominance regime, and if Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's jawboning fails, his backup includes expanded Fed reserve management purchases, bank deregulation to free balance-sheet capacity for Treasuries, and possibly Fed yield caps justified under the Fed's rarely cited 'moderate long-term interest rates' mandate.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Long-end yield spikes are likely to be capped by policy, a tailwind for risk assets and debasement hedges.
insights.quote: So, there's the Bessin bluff, but I think it's backed up by the Bessant bazooka.

insights.claim: Anthony Pompliano frames Bessent's $6 billion Treasury buybacks as insurgent-style probing of market pressure points, with far more firepower held in reserve if the market keeps calling his bluff.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Small initial buybacks should be read as a signal test, not the ceiling of intervention.

insights.claim: Dale cites Bessent intervening alongside Japan's Ministry of Finance to defend the yen as evidence the Treasury Secretary recognizes the Treasury-market supply-demand imbalance, and calls him possibly the best-fit Treasury Secretary of the modern era.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Coordinated US-Japan FX action signals willingness to backstop Japanese demand for US assets; watch USD/JPY interventions.
insights.quote: Why else would you be intervening alongside Japan's Ministry of Finance to defend the yen?

insights.claim: Pompliano's working theory is that Bessent encouraged Stanley Druckenmiller's widely discussed (reportedly AI-written) op-ed so that a trusted friend could publicly say what the Treasury Secretary believes but cannot say; Dale adds the outcome, more public pressure on DC, is the same either way.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Druckenmiller's public views may be a proxy for Treasury thinking on fiscal/debt policy.

themes.theme: Stocks at highs despite bad headlines

insights.claim: Darius Dale expects US stocks to make significant new highs over the next 12-18 months and says the bull market is not over, because the Treasury imbalance forces ongoing policy intervention/monetary debasement while AI capex supplies an orthogonal earnings tailwind.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Stay long equities; 42 Macro sees macro headwinds as reasons for intervention, not for a bear market.
insights.quote: it's one of the reasons why we think stocks will go to make significant highs from here uh over the next 12 to 18 months. In our view, we don't think this bull market is over.

insights.claim: Against Pompliano's scenario of $100 oil, 5% 10-year yields, a Fed hike, geopolitical conflict, and an AI-only economy, Dale argues stocks should be at all-time highs precisely because those conditions force policy intervention.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Bad macro data is bullish for assets in a fiscal-dominance regime; do not sell risk on stagflationary headlines alone.
insights.quote: I would actually argue that stocks would probably be at all times because of some of the dynamics you listed.

insights.claim: Dale cites hyperscaler AI capex of about $800 billion next year growing toward $1.2-1.4 trillion, calling it a 'massive AI capex bubble' that is nonetheless a powerful earnings tailwind.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure spending remains the main earnings driver; its reversal is a key risk to the bull case.
insights.quote: This is massive AI capex bubble. You're talking $800 billion in hyperscala capex next year

insights.claim: 42 Macro has been structurally bullish since January 2023 except February-April 2025, when it viewed the deficit-cutting 'paradigm B' as negative, then pivoted back to bullish once policy shifted to running the economy hot.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Track record context: 42 Macro's regime calls key off fiscal posture (cut vs. grow).

insights.claim: Dale says the main thing that would end the bull market is a lack of the required policy intervention, such as a serious pivot back to deficit-cutting, which he rates a very low-probability bet; Pompliano concludes no one will ever balance the budget, implying recessions and prolonged downturns will be policy-suppressed.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Watch for genuine fiscal austerity as the key bear signal, not bad economic data.

insights.claim: In fall 2024, 42 Macro replaced the 30% bond allocation in its KISS model portfolio with gold, on the view that neither Republicans nor Democrats were serious about balancing the budget; Dale called DOGE 'Kabuki theater'.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: An explicit gold-over-bonds allocation as a hedge against fiscal indiscipline.
insights.quote: we replaced our 30% allocation to bonds with gold in our in our flagship uh asset allocation, our KISS model portfolio.

insights.claim: Dale's framework for escaping the 'debt disease': paradigm B (cut the deficit), paradigm C (grow nominal GDP faster than debt), paradigm D (print/default via debasement), plus the bad options of outright default and total war; only cutting reduces political dysfunction, since the others end in inflation.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: A regime map for positioning: current paradigm C favors equities; a shift to D favors hard assets and debasement hedges.

insights.claim: The US is succeeding at paradigm C, with nominal GDP ex-government and net exports growing about 8% in the most recent quarter versus a pre-COVID mean of 4%, and Dale's research suggests this growth phase lasts at least to 2028 and maybe beyond.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Supports a multi-year pro-risk window; the transition to paradigm D (printing) is the long-term regime-change risk.

insights.claim: Dale expects that when growth runs out the government will print via relaxed bank regulation, yield curve control, or expanded reserve management purchases, and he considers all of these money printing.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Long-term debasement thesis supportive of gold and Bitcoin as monetary hedges.
insights.quote: I don't know. Who cares? It's all money printing.

insights.claim: Dale notes the Fed has cut about 175 basis points while missing its inflation target for five consecutive years (projected nine), and has monetized sovereign debt amid a nationwide affordability crisis.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Signals the Fed is prioritizing debt financing over its inflation target, a dovish bias that favors real assets.

insights.claim: Dale expects re-industrialization to force a choice over who absorbs higher costs, the capital class via margin compression or W2 workers via higher inflation; Pompliano counters that automation, as with Tesla cutting prices from ~$120K to ~$40K, can preserve margins without either absorbing the cost, though few businesses can replicate it.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Onshoring is either margin-dilutive or inflationary unless automation scales; watch corporate margins vs CPI.
insights.quote: who's going to eat the additional cost of goods and services, is it going to be the K1 class via margin compression or is it going to be the K the W2 class via higher inflation?

insights.claim: Dale's analysis of Treasury budget data finds about 36% of the ~$8 trillion in federal spending goes to the wealthy (including ~$1.1-1.2T net interest and ~$1T net defense to defense suppliers such as SpaceX and Palantir) versus about 17% (~$1.2-1.3T means-tested programs) to the poor, a 'reverse Robin Hood effect' or 'wealth pump'.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Net interest and defense outlays are structural income streams to asset holders and defense contractors.

insights.claim: Dale warns that if paradigm C growth runs out and policy shifts to printing from a starting point where 7 in 10 US households live paycheck to paycheck (citing a JPMorgan economist), a major political realignment is likely, with MAGA and DSA converging and total war a high-probability outcome.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Tail risk: populist realignment could bring wealth redistribution or margin-targeting policy hostile to capital holders.
insights.quote: I think total war is a high probability outcome in that scenario as well.

insights.claim: Dale's core thesis is that the US has become so good at generating profits for the capital (K1) class that it has come at the expense of W2 income, savings, home-buying and mobility, undermining societal stability.
insights.speaker: Darius Dale
insights.so_what: Record profit margins face political mean-reversion risk over time.
insights.quote: we've gotten so good at creating profits in this society that we've probably overdone it.

insights.claim: Pompliano argues Bitcoin (an army of compute defending against money printing) and AI (giving every individual Bill Gates-in-the-1990s-level intellectual horsepower within 12-24 months) are the technologies that can lift people out of the K-shaped squeeze.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Pompliano's case for Bitcoin as a retail debasement hedge in a printing regime.
insights.quote: It creates all these computers that work for you to defend your economic value.
